title: Lamentations 2:1–10
context: The poet describes the destruction of the daughter of Zion: the Lord has covered her with a cloud in his anger, cast down the beauty of Israel, swallowed up dwellings and strongholds, cut off Israel’s horn, and stood with his bow like an enemy. “The Lord has become as an enemy.” Tabernacle, assembly, altar, and sanctuary are cast off; the enemy has made a noise in the LORD’s house; the wall is marked for destroying; gates have sunk; king, princes, and prophets are gone or sightless; elders sit on the ground in silence and sackcloth, and the young women of Jerusalem hang down their heads. The wrath and the grief, including the LORD “like an enemy” and “as an enemy” are shared ground: the simile names the severity of the blow, while the lament still addresses him as Lord. God is not being called the author of sin. How God relates to agents of judgment may be compared, where it helps, with Judges 9:23, without restating that discussion. The ruined sanctuary and the public mourning should be treated with pastoral care. 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 narrate the fall, and Deuteronomy 28 names covenant curses; those texts may be named by reference without being blended here.

verses.text: How has the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud in his anger! He has cast the beauty of Israel down from heaven to the earth, and hasn’t remembered his footstool in the day of his anger.
verses.arminianNotes:
“How has the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud in his anger!” The beauty of Israel has been cast down from heaven to the earth, and his footstool has not been remembered in the day of his anger. The cry matches the “How” of 1:1, now aimed at anger that covers and casts down. “footstool” is often taken of the sanctuary or of the city as the place of his feet; the verse does not define it, and that may be hedged.

Arminian readers hear a real lament over anger that has covered Zion like a cloud, a fall from beauty, which the poet is right to tell without first resolving every image.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same covering cloud, the casting down of Israel’s beauty, and the unremembered footstool in the day of his anger, as the poet’s opening account of this chapter’s destruction.

Shared ground: the day of his anger is the subject. Wrath and grief are not a fork here.

verses.text: The Lord has swallowed up all the dwellings of Jacob without pity. He has thrown down in his wrath the strongholds of the daughter of Judah. He has brought them down to the ground. He has profaned the kingdom and its princes.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord has swallowed up the dwellings of Jacob without pity, thrown down the strongholds of the daughter of Judah, brought them to the ground, and profaned the kingdom and its princes. The verbs are the Lord’s; the objects are homes, strongholds, kingdom, and princes. “without pity” belongs to the lament’s frankness, and should be heard as such, not softened and not sensationalized.

Arminian readers hear a comprehensive throwing-down, named without pity because that is how it felt and how the poet tells it, a grief that still speaks to the Lord who has done this.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same swallowing up, the strongholds thrown down, and the profaning of the kingdom and princes, as the Lord’s work in wrath, told in the poet’s third-person report.

Shared ground: the destruction is described as the Lord’s, and the lack of pity is the verse’s own word. The traditions can share that hardness of description.

verses.text: He has cut off all the horn of Israel in fierce anger. He has drawn back his right hand from before the enemy. He has burned up Jacob like a flaming fire, which devours all around.
verses.arminianNotes:
In fierce anger, the poet says, the horn of Israel has been cut off; the right hand has been drawn back from before the enemy; Jacob has been burned like a flaming fire that devours all around. The “horn” is a common image of strength; it may be left as such, without a forced identification. The drawn-back right hand is the withdrawal of the help that might have met the enemy.

Arminian readers hear both the loss of strength and the withdrawal of the defending hand, a fierce anger the people now live under, which the lament may name and still bring to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the cut-off horn, the drawn-back right hand, and the fire that burns up Jacob, as the poet’s account of fierce anger at work in the fall.

Shared ground: strength is gone, and the enemy is not held back. There is no party contrast over the images.

verses.text: He has bent his bow like an enemy. He has stood with his right hand as an adversary. He has killed all that were pleasant to the eye. In the tent of the daughter of Zion, he has poured out his wrath like fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
The poet says he has bent his bow “like an enemy” and has stood with his right hand “as an adversary” and has killed all that were pleasant to the eye. In the tent of the daughter of Zion, wrath has been poured out like fire. The similes “like an enemy” and “as an adversary” are the verse’s way of telling how severe the blow felt. They are shared ground, not a claim that the Lord is morally an evildoer, and not a new contrast over salvation. The killing of what was pleasant to the eye should be named only as briefly and carefully as the line itself.

Arminian readers hear the likeness to an enemy as the truth of Zion’s experience in this day of wrath, a likeness the poem is allowed to use while still speaking of the Lord’s own wrath.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the bent bow, the right hand as an adversary, and the wrath poured out like fire in Zion’s tent, as the poet’s report of the Lord’s opposing stance in judgment.

Shared ground: “like an enemy” names the severity of the act, not a change in God’s holiness. Both traditions can stay with the lament.

verses.text: The Lord has become as an enemy. He has swallowed up Israel. He has swallowed up all her palaces. He has destroyed his strongholds. He has multiplied mourning and lamentation in the daughter of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The Lord has become as an enemy.” The verse then tells of Israel swallowed up, palaces swallowed up, strongholds destroyed, and mourning and lamentation multiplied in the daughter of Judah. The “as an enemy” matches verse 4 and should be read in the same sober way: the Lord has taken the place of an opponent in this judgment, and the mourning is multiplied. God remains the one the book addresses; he is not being recast as the author of sin.

Arminian readers hear a hard confession of experience—the Lord has become as an enemy—joined to a catalogue of swallowed palaces and multiplied lament, which the poet tells so that the grief is not denied.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “as an enemy” the swallowing up of Israel and her palaces, and the multiplied mourning, as the Lord’s judgment told from the poet’s side.

Shared ground: the simile and the mourning belong together. This is not a soteriological fork, and it need not restate a debate about a believer’s standing.

verses.text: He has violently taken away his tabernacle, as if it were a garden. He has destroyed his place of assembly. The LORD has caused solemn assembly and Sabbath to be forgotten in Zion. In the indignation of his anger, he has despised the king and the priest.
verses.arminianNotes:
His tabernacle has been violently taken away, as if it were a garden; his place of assembly has been destroyed. “The LORD has caused solemn assembly and Sabbath to be forgotten in Zion.” In the indignation of his anger, king and priest have been despised. The lost worship—tabernacle, assembly, Sabbath—is at the heart of this verse and should be treated as a holy loss, with care.

Arminian readers hear the dismantling of the place and the times of meeting, assembly and Sabbath forgotten, a wound to the life of worship that the lament is right to name beside the city’s other ruins.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the taken tabernacle, the destroyed place of assembly, the forgotten solemn assembly and Sabbath, and the despised king and priest, as the LORD’s doing in the indignation of his anger.

Shared ground: Zion’s worship has been made to cease. 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52 may be named for the fall of the house, without blending the accounts here.

verses.text: The Lord has cast off his altar. He has abhorred his sanctuary. He has given the walls of her palaces into the hand of the enemy. They have made a noise in the LORD’s house, as in the day of a solemn assembly.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The Lord has cast off his altar.” The sanctuary, the poet says, has been abhorred, and the walls of her palaces have been given into the enemy’s hand. They have made a noise in the LORD’s house, as in the day of a solemn assembly. The altar and the sanctuary are his, and they are rejected; the noise in the house is a grim parody of a feast day. This should be told as the ruin of holy things, without expansion into a scene.

Arminian readers hear the casting off of the altar and the noise in the LORD’s house as a real desecration, a grief over worship turned to an enemy’s shout, which the poem sets beside the fallen walls.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same rejected altar and sanctuary, the palaces given to the enemy, and the noise in the LORD’s house as in a solemn assembly, as the Lord’s own casting off, told by the poet.

Shared ground: the holy house has been given over. Pastoral restraint is required, and the traditions share the grief.

verses.text: The LORD has purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion. He has stretched out the line. He has not withdrawn his hand from destroying; He has made the rampart and wall lament. They languish together.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD has purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion.” A line has been stretched out; the hand has not been withdrawn from destroying; rampart and wall lament and languish together. The wall itself is pictured as mourning. The destruction is purposed, not accidental, and both traditions hear the poet ascribing it to the LORD.

Arminian readers hear a purposed destroying of the wall, a relentless hand, and even the rampart lamenting, a scene of civic ruin the lament may tell as purpose and as grief together.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same purpose to destroy the wall, the stretched line, and the rampart and wall languishing together, as the LORD’s deliberate work against Zion’s defenses.

Shared ground: the wall falls by purpose. Deuteronomy 28 may be named as a background of warned ruin, without claiming that this verse is only a citation of that chapter.

verses.text: Her gates have sunk into the ground. He has destroyed and broken her bars. Her king and her princes are among the nations where the law is not. Yes, her prophets find no vision from the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Her gates have sunk into the ground.” Her bars are destroyed and broken; her king and her princes are among the nations “where the law is not.” Her prophets find no vision from the LORD. The exact force of “where the law is not” may be hedged: among peoples who do not have that law, or in a condition where the law is not in force as it was. The silence of vision is part of the same loss.

Arminian readers hear gates sunk, leaders in exile, and prophets without a vision, a threefold emptiness that the people now live in, and that need not be turned into a theory of prophecy before it can be mourned.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the sunk gates, the broken bars, the king and princes among the nations, and the prophets who find no vision from the LORD, as the poet’s account of civic, royal, and prophetic collapse.

Shared ground: gate, law, and vision have failed together. The phrase about the law is explained only modestly.

verses.text: The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground. They keep silence. They have cast up dust on their heads. They have clothed themselves with sackcloth. The virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground. They keep silence. They have cast up dust on their heads. They have clothed themselves with sackcloth. The virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground.” The unit ends in a public posture of mourning: silence, dust, sackcloth, and heads bowed. The young women of Jerusalem should be mentioned only as the verse mentions them, with care, as part of the city’s grief, not as a cue for other comment.

Arminian readers hear a community that has sat down in silence and dust, elders and young women together in mourning, a sight the poet leaves in place as the close of the destruction report.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same sitting, silence, dust, sackcloth, and bowed heads as the visible answer to the destruction just described.

Shared ground: the city mourns on the ground. The verse is a quiet close, and both traditions can stay quiet with it.
